cloze.en: Hello, I'm Emre. Nice to meet you!

words.notes: Works with anyone at any time of day, though 'Guten Tag' is safer with strangers and officials.

example_sentences.de: Guten Morgen, haben Sie gut geschlafen?
example_sentences.en: Good morning, did you sleep well?

cloze.en: Good morning! Would you like a coffee?

words.notes: Used until about 10 or 11 am. Often shortened to just 'Morgen!' among colleagues.

example_sentences.de: Guten Tag, ich habe einen Termin.
Guten Tag, was kann ich für Sie tun?
example_sentences.en: Hello, what can I do for you?

words.notes: The safe, neutral greeting for any stranger, shop, office or doctor.
words.germany_context: Germans greet on entering a small shop, a waiting room or a lift. Saying nothing reads as rude.

example_sentences.de: Guten Abend, ein Tisch für zwei bitte.
example_sentences.en: Good evening, a table for two please.

example_sentences.de: Guten Abend, schön Sie zu sehen.
example_sentences.en: Good evening, nice to see you.

cloze.en: Good evening! How was your day?

words.notes: From roughly 6 pm. A greeting, not a farewell.

example_sentences.de: Ich gehe ins Bett. Gute Nacht!
example_sentences.en: I'm going to bed. Good night!

words.notes: Only when someone is going to bed — never as a general evening greeting.

example_sentences.en: Hi there, are you coming along?

words.germany_context: Hamburg, Bremen and the whole north. Despite sounding like 'Morgen' it's used all day long. Saying 'Moin moin' twice is considered chatty.

example_sentences.de: Grüß Gott, was darf es sein?
example_sentences.en: Hello, what can I get you?

words.germany_context: Bavaria and Austria. Literally 'greet God', but it carries no religious weight at all — it is simply the normal hello there.

words.notes: Works as both hello and goodbye, but only informally.

example_sentences.en: Bye and have a nice weekend!

words.notes: Informal but extremely common — even shop staff use it.

example_sentences.en: Goodbye and thank you very much!

words.notes: The formal goodbye. On the phone Germans say 'Auf Wiederhören' instead — you'll hear again rather than see again.

example_sentences.de: Bis bald, war schön dich zu sehen!
example_sentences.en: See you soon, it was nice to see you!

words.notes: The same pattern gives you bis später (see you later), bis morgen (see you tomorrow), bis nächste Woche.

example_sentences.en: See you tomorrow at the office!

cloze.en: Have a nice evening, see you tomorrow!
Thank you very much. — Have a nice day!

words.notes: The standard sign-off at any counter. The reply is 'Danke, ebenfalls!' or 'Gleichfalls!'

example_sentences.en: Have a nice weekend, see you Monday!
You have a nice weekend too!

cloze.en: See you Monday and have a nice weekend!

words.germany_context: Said to everyone on a Friday — colleagues, the baker, the bus driver. Not saying it back feels cold.

example_sentences.en: Have a nice weekend! — Thanks, you too!

cloze.en: Have a nice day! — Thanks, you too!

words.notes: 'Ebenfalls' means exactly the same. Both are the standard reply to any good wish.
Does triple duty: 'please', 'you're welcome', and 'here you go' when handing something over.
Careful: after 'vielen' or 'herzlichen' it becomes 'Dank' — vielen Dank, herzlichen Dank.

example_sentences.en: Thank you very much for your help!

example_sentences.de: Vielen Dank, das ist sehr nett.
example_sentences.en: Thank you very much, that's very kind.

cloze.de: ___ Dank, Sie haben mir sehr geholfen.
cloze.en: Thank you very much, you helped me a lot.

words.notes: 'Danke schön' and 'Herzlichen Dank' are equally good.

example_sentences.en: Thank you very much! — You're welcome!

words.notes: 'Bitte', 'Kein Problem' and 'Gerne' all work as replies to thanks too.

example_sentences.de: Bitte schön, hier ist Ihr Kaffee.
example_sentences.en: Here you go, here's your coffee.

cloze.en: Here you go, here's your receipt.

words.notes: Said as things are handed over. 'Danke schön' / 'Bitte schön' pair up naturally.

example_sentences.de: Guten Tag, wie geht es Ihnen?

words.notes: Ihnen is the formal dative — always capitalised when it means 'you'.
words.germany_context: Unlike in English, this is a real question, not a greeting. Germans give an honest answer, so be ready for more than 'fine'.

words.notes: Short for 'Wie geht es dir?'. Only with people you say du to.

example_sentences.de: Mir geht es gut, danke. Und Ihnen?

cloze.de: ___ geht es gut, danke der Nachfrage.

words.notes: Literally 'to me it goes well' — this construction uses the dative 'mir', never 'ich'.
Dative again: 'dir' informally, 'Ihnen' formally. Not 'du' or 'Sie'.

example_sentences.de: Ich heiße Anna. — Freut mich, Emre.
example_sentences.en: My name is Anna. — Nice to meet you, I'm Emre.
It's a pleasure to meet you.

cloze.en: This is my colleague. — Nice to meet you!

words.notes: Short for 'Es freut mich, Sie kennenzulernen'. Usually said with a handshake.
words.germany_context: A firm handshake with eye contact is standard on first meeting, in both social and work settings.

words.notes: Informally: 'Wie heißt du?'. 'Wie ist Ihr Name?' is also common in offices.

example_sentences.de: Woher kommen Sie? — Aus der Türkei.
example_sentences.en: Where are you from? — From Turkey.

cloze.en: Where are you from? — From Istanbul.

words.notes: woher = where FROM. Don't confuse it with wo (where something is) or wohin (where to).
Always 'Glückwunsch zu' + dative: zum Geburtstag, zur Hochzeit.
words.germany_context: Never congratulate a German on a birthday BEFORE the day — it's widely considered bad luck.

example_sentences.en: All the best for your birthday!
All the best for the future!

cloze.en: All the best and good luck!

example_sentences.en: Good luck with the job interview!

cloze.en: Good luck with the appointment tomorrow!

words.notes: 'Viel Erfolg!' is used where effort rather than luck decides — exams, interviews, presentations.

example_sentences.en: Get well soon, get some rest!

example_sentences.de: Ich bin krank. — Oh, gute Besserung!
example_sentences.en: I'm ill. — Oh, get well soon!

example_sentences.de: Gute Reise und komm gut an!
example_sentences.en: Have a good trip and arrive safely!
I'm flying tomorrow. — Have a good trip!

cloze.en: Have a good trip and see you soon!

example_sentences.de: Frohe Weihnachten und ein gutes neues Jahr!
example_sentences.en: Merry Christmas and a happy new year!

words.germany_context: Germans celebrate on the evening of the 24th (Heiligabend), not the morning of the 25th. Almost everything shuts from midday on the 24th.

example_sentences.de: Frohes neues Jahr! Alles Gute für 2026!
example_sentences.en: Happy New Year! All the best for 2026!
Have a good slide into the new year!

words.notes: Before New Year's Eve Germans say 'Guten Rutsch!' — literally 'good slide'.
Used for all adult women regardless of marital status. 'Fräulein' is long obsolete and sounds insulting.

example_sentences.de: Entschuldigen Sie bitte, wo ist der Ausgang?
example_sentences.en: Excuse me please, where is the exit?

cloze.de: ___ Sie bitte, ist dieser Platz frei?
cloze.en: Excuse me please, is this seat free?

words.notes: Slightly more formal than plain 'Entschuldigung'.

example_sentences.de: Darf ich vorstellen: das ist meine Kollegin Anna.
example_sentences.en: May I introduce: this is my colleague Anna.

example_sentences.de: Darf ich Ihnen Herrn Weber vorstellen?
example_sentences.en: May I introduce Mr Weber to you?

cloze.de: Darf ich ___: das ist mein Bruder.
cloze.en: May I introduce: this is my brother.

words.notes: vorstellen is separable, but here it sits at the end already because of 'darf'.

words.translation: Have a nice evening after work!
translations: Have a nice evening after work!

example_sentences.en: See you tomorrow, have a nice evening!

cloze.en: Bye, have a nice evening after work!

words.notes: Feierabend is the time after work — there's no single English word for it.
words.germany_context: Feierabend is close to sacred. Once the working day ends, colleagues genuinely stop contacting each other, and that is respected rather than resented.

example_sentences.de: Sehr geehrte Damen und Herren, ich schreibe Ihnen wegen meiner Bewerbung.
example_sentences.en: Dear Sir or Madam, I am writing regarding my application.

example_sentences.de: Sehr geehrte Frau Meyer, vielen Dank für Ihre Nachricht.
example_sentences.en: Dear Ms Meyer, thank you for your message.

words.notes: The standard opening of any formal letter or email. Sign off with 'Mit freundlichen Grüßen'.

example_sentences.en: Best wishes and see you soon!

words.notes: Formal. Among colleagues and friends: 'Viele Grüße', 'Liebe Grüße' or just 'LG'.

example_sentences.de: Wir arbeiten jetzt zusammen — können wir uns duzen?
example_sentences.en: We work together now — shall we use 'du'?

words.notes: duzen = to say du. siezen = to say Sie.
words.germany_context: The switch from Sie to du is offered by the older person, the woman, or the more senior colleague. Wait to be offered rather than assuming — but in startups and among under-30s, du is usually immediate.

example_sentences.de: Hey, lange nicht gesehen! Wie geht's?
example_sentences.en: Hey, long time no see! How are you?

example_sentences.de: Wir haben uns lange nicht gesehen.
example_sentences.en: We haven't seen each other in a long time.

example_sentences.de: Sorry, ich muss los — mein Zug fährt gleich.
example_sentences.en: Sorry, I have to go — my train leaves shortly.

example_sentences.de: Es ist schon spät, ich muss langsam los.
example_sentences.en: It's late, I should get going.

cloze.en: It's late, I have to go.

words.notes: The natural, friendly way to leave a conversation.

example_sentences.de: Melden Sie sich, wenn Sie Fragen haben.
example_sentences.en: Get in touch if you have questions.

cloze.en: See you soon and get in touch!

words.notes: sich melden = to get in touch. The 'mal' just softens it — it's very common and adds no real meaning.

example_sentences.de: Wir sollten uns mal auf einen Kaffee treffen.
example_sentences.en: We should meet up for a coffee sometime.

words.germany_context: Unlike the English version, a German usually means this literally — expect them to follow up and propose an actual date.

example_sentences.de: Ich gehe ins Kino. — Viel Spaß!
example_sentences.en: I'm going to the cinema. — Have fun!

words.notes: 'Herzlich willkommen' is the full, warmer form you'll see on signs.
